phonemes.desc: Initial syllable with postalveolar approximant [j] and central vowel [ʊə] — the name opens with the same glide heard in English 'yes' followed by a soft, rounded r-coloured vowel.
Alveolar lateral [l] plus open-mid back vowel [ʊ] and alveolar nasal [n]; the middle syllable is level and unaccented in the Yolŋu song register.
Voiced velar stop [ɡ] followed by central r-coloured vowel [ʊə]; the final syllable carries the weight of the word in English scholarly pronunciation.

pronunciation.approximation: 'YUR-lun-gur' — three level syllables, with the first syllable receiving a light stress. Keep the 'r' soft; this is an anglicized scholarly rendering of a Yolŋu name.

pronunciation.note: The ideal form would preserve Yolŋu retroflex or postalveolar phonemes, but these are not registrable in the DNS root zone. PuniCodex therefore records the conventional English scholarly spelling **Yurlungur** with initial capitalization. The name is Tier 2: the restoration capitalizes the proper noun but does not add a diacritic or distinctive letter that the ASCII form lacks, because the Aboriginal source is transmitted orally and is conventionally romanized without special marks.

domains.title: The Great Copper Python
domains.subtitle: Initiation, Law, and the Rainbow Serpent
domains.lead: Yurlungur is the great copper python of the Yolŋu peoples of northeast Arnhem Land — a Rainbow Serpent whose swallowing of the boy Wawi at the first circumcision became the template for male initiation across the Murngin world. He is not merely a monster; he is the law itself, the waterhole guardian, and the ancestor who transforms boys into men.

cards.name: Initiation
cards.desc: Yurlungur swallows the novice and releases him as a man; his waterhole is the first borum ground.

cards.name: Rainbow Serpent
cards.desc: The copper snake whose body arcs across sky and waterhole, binding rain, fertility, and ancestral power.

cards.name: Guardian of Waterholes
cards.desc: He dwells in the deep sacred wells; to disturb them is to risk drought, flood, and sickness.

cards.name: Ancestral Law
cards.desc: His story encodes the rules of food taboo, kinship, and ritual obligation that hold Yolŋu society together.

mythology.lead: The central Yurlungur myth is an initiation narrative: a boy breaks a food prohibition, is swallowed by the great copper python, and is restored to his kin only after the correct ritual response. In that single event the whole logic of Yolŋu male initiation — death to childhood, passage through the ancestor's body, rebirth as a man — is enacted for the first time.

myths.title: The Swallowing of Wawi
myths.text: At the first borum (circumcision) ceremony, the boy Wawi ate food that had been forbidden to him. The great copper snake Yurlungur rose from his waterhole and swallowed the boy whole. The other ancestors were dismayed; the boy's mother followed his tracks to the waterhole and wept. Moved — or perhaps shamed — by her grief, Yurlungur vomited the boy out, alive but transformed. From that day the pattern was set: every novice must enter the ancestral body and emerge again.

myths.title: The Mother at the Waterhole
myths.text: The mother's pursuit is as important as the snake's swallowing. She traces Wawi to the edge of the sacred pool, the place where the human world opens into the ancestral realm. Her tears and her knowledge of the law are what compel Yurlungur to release the boy. The story thus encodes the partnership of male and female knowledge in initiation: men operate the ritual, but women hold the relational power that makes return possible.

myths.title: The First Borum Ground
myths.text: After Wawi's return, the ground around Yurlungur's waterhole became the prototype of the borum ground — the cleared ceremonial space where initiates are separated from women and children, painted with ochre, and introduced to the sacred objects of adulthood. The snake's body becomes the template of the initiatory enclosure: a dangerous, transformative space from which one must not emerge unchanged.

myths.title: Rainbow Serpent Typology
myths.text: Yurlungur belongs to the Rainbow Serpent family that stretches across Aboriginal Australia — Ngalyod in western Arnhem Land, the Waugal of the southwest, the Wanambi of the central deserts. Like them he links water, fertility, and ancestral law; unlike some regional forms he is specifically tied to male initiation and to the copper-coloured python that gives him his name.

lore.syncretism: Yurlungur is best understood within the Yolŋu moieties (Dhuwa and Yirritja) and the clan-specific song cycles (manikay) that map his journeys between waterholes. He is not a universal Aboriginal god but a regional ancestor whose story is owned and transmitted by particular Yolŋu lineages. Comparative anthropologists have grouped him with Rainbow Serpent figures across the continent, yet Yolŋu custodians emphasize the local specificity of his name, sites, and ritual obligations. In modern discourse he appears in Indigenous land-rights testimony, in museum interpretations of Arnhem Land art, and in scholarly discussions of Aboriginal religion and environmental knowledge.
lore.culturalLegacy: Yurlungur remains a living ancestor for Yolŋu peoples. His story is performed in initiation, painted in bark paintings and on bodies, and invoked in claims to country and water. Anthropologists from Warner and the Berndts onward have used the Murngin material as a classic case study in Australian Aboriginal religion, kinship, and ritual. In wider Australian culture, the Rainbow Serpent — including figures such as Yurlungur — has become an emblem of Indigenous ecological knowledge and the deep connection between sacred law and the care of water. Contemporary Yolŋu artists continue to depict the great copper python, and his name is cited in discussions of cultural heritage, repatriation, and Indigenous intellectual property.
lore.extendedMeditation:
Yurlungur asks us to think about transformation as something that happens through the body of an ancestor rather than through individual will. The boy does not choose to be swallowed; the law chooses him. He does not engineer his own rebirth; his mother's grief, the snake's response, and the community's ritual competence restore him. Initiation is therefore not a personal achievement but a social event: the whole kinship system must hold for one person to change.

In a world that prizes autonomy, Yurlungur offers a counter-image of becoming. To become a man is to be eaten by the law, to lose the name one had as a child, and to be returned with obligations one did not choose. The snake is frightening not because he is cruel but because he is impersonal: he enforces the taboo whether the boy understands it or not. Yet he is also the guardian of water, the bringer of rain, and the ancestor who makes the country habitable. His fierceness and his generosity are the same thing.
lore.originalScriptNote: Yurlungur is transmitted orally in Yolŋu Matha and was first recorded in English-based orthographies by anthropologists in the early twentieth century. There is no single Indigenous script corresponding to the name; the forms Yurlungur, Yulunggur, Julunggul, and Yurluŋgur represent different transcription conventions and clan pronunciations. The PuniCodex restoration capitalizes the conventional scholarly romanization as a proper noun. Because the ASCII form yurlungur already encodes the same romanized sequence without distinctive diacritics or special letters, the name is classified Tier 2.

etymology.derivation: The name is generally interpreted in the scholarly literature as 'great copper snake' or 'copper python', from Yolŋu words for the coloured serpent associated with waterholes and rain. The exact morphemic analysis is uncertain because the name is a proper noun preserved in oral tradition rather than a transparent compound.

lore.archaeology: The material evidence for Yurlungur is held in Yolŋu ceremonial objects, rock art, and sacred sites rather than in excavated strata. Bark paintings from northeast Arnhem Land depict the Rainbow Serpent and the initiation complex; notable collections are held by the Australian Institute of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Studies (AIATSIS), the National Museum of Australia, and the Museum and Art Gallery of the Northern Territory. The waterholes identified as Yurlungur's dwelling remain active sacred sites, and access to them is governed by Yolŋu customary law. Archaeological research in the region has documented long-term Aboriginal occupation of the Arnhem Land plateau and adjacent coastal plains, providing the environmental context within which the Yurlungur narratives are embedded.
